## Introduction

Links to github https://github.com/psych251/nolte2025

Link to original paper https://github.com/psych251/nolte2025/tree/main/original_paper

I chose to examine this study because it examines a key theme in my research: how does aging affect the processes by which we engage with information in order to make - or avoid - important decisions.  The study provides a variety of setting in which older and younger adults make decisions, including choosing a physician, a health insurance plan, housing, and purchasing a car. Additionally, the authors sought to understand whether affect or cognition might account for age-related differences in decision making and avoidance. Half of the subjects completed a writing intervention task designed to decrease decision-making avoidance. 

## Methods
The original paper consisted of two studies; here, we replicate Study 2 of the paper to examine whether a writing intervention might decrease avoidance. The study recruited 501 participants (448 via Qualrtics, 52 via laboratory participation). The final sample consisted of 479 participants aged 18-96, in which 51% of the sample identified as women and 65% of the sample identified as Non-Hispanic White. 

Survey materials and data are accessible via the study's Open Science Framework pre-registration.
https://osf.io/7wupg/?view_only=1e7ee013faf040088d6665008d3e2aef

### Power Analysis

Here, we aim to recruit approximately 40 particiants per cell (2 age groups (Young Adult - Older Adult) × 2 conditions (Intervention - No intervention); N = 160). This estimates a 96% power for the original control-condition effect (d = 0.85); at a standard 80% power, an effect of d = 0.63 is still detectable. We will test 1. age differences within condition (described above), the main effect of age across both conditions, and the main effect of intervention. Because the interaction would require testing n=620 participants total at 80% power, we wil not be testing for the age*condition interaction. 

### Planned Sample

Size: 160 participants (40 per cell). Recruiting about 176 to allow for exclusions / drop outs. 
Ages: Younger adults 18–35 and older adults 66 and older (to match the original's age-group definitions).
Eligibility: Engligh-speaking U.S. residents, recruited through Prolific 
Recruitment: Prolific, using two separate study recruitment postings (one for each age group). Condition is assigned randomly within age group by the embedded Qualtrics randomizer. 
Compensation: Participants are paid $2 for an estimated 13 minute study (the equivalent of 9.23 hourly, below Prolific's recommended 26/hour compensation and above the federal minimum wage of 7.25 per hour.) For both studies (n=80, rate is 2/hr, cost = 213) the total cost is 426 USD. 

### Materials

All materials come from the original Study 2 Qualtrics survey ("2023 Decision Avoidance II"), with the unrelated measures removed (see differences from original study section). 
- Demographics: age, gender, U.S. residence, race/ethnic group, education (5 levels), household income (7 levels); year of birth as an age-consistency check.
- Baseline affect: valence (1 = Very negative, 7 = Very positive) and arousal (1 = Very quiet/still, 7 = Very activated/aroused).
- Goals and life position: growth vs. maintenance goals and information vs. affect goals (0–100 sliders, midpoint 50); perceived life position (0 = Birth, 100 = Death).
- Self-rated health and cognition: physical health, emotional health, learning ability, memory (1 = Poor, 5 = Excellent). 
- Maximization scale: 6 items, Nenkov et al. (2008).
- Numeracy: 3 Lipkus et al. (2001) items (0–3 correct), plus a fourth door-prize item used as an attention check (correct answer 1,000).
- Personality: 10-item Big Five Inventory (Rammstedt & John, 2007).
- Decision avoidance task: four scenarios (apartment, car, physician, health plan) in random order. Participants choose an option or "Not choose any of these [options] for the time being." Outcome = number avoided, 0–4.
- Peri-decisional ratings (1–7): difficulty, effort, stress, anticipated regret.
- Post-decisional ratings (1–7): valence, arousal, satisfaction, regret.
- Writing intervention (intervention condition only): before rating and choosing, "Please write down what you like and dislike about each option," in a text box beside the option grid.


### Procedure	

The procedure is described as follows, in the words of the paper, "The survey assessed participants' demographic background, baseline affect, life goals, perceived life position, self-rated health and cognitive abilities, maximization tendencies, numeracy skills, and personality traits, in that order. Participants then responded to all four decision avoidance tasks in randomized order. The survey ended after participants reported their birth year". 
The decision avoidance task was comprised of four scenarios (apartment, car, physician, health plan) in random order. Half of the participants are randomly assigned to a writing condition before and after selecting their decision, in which they respond to the prompt "Please write down what you like and dislike about each option" beside the option grid. 

### Analysis Plan

Data are processed with the original authors' Study 2 script (Decision_Avoidance_2_Studies_2025 Updated N479.R). 

**Clarify key analysis of interest here**  Here, we aim to examine whether 1. age differences in decision avoidance replicate from the original study, and 2. if the intervention drives differences in peri- and post-decisional affect and / or cognitive load. We examine age, decision avoidance across scenarios (0-4), affect, and cognition. 

### Differences from Original Study

Due to budgeting constraints, we aim to recruit at the ends of the adult lifespan sample (ie, 18-35, and ages 66+) rather than a full lifespan sample including midlife. We chose to do this to see age effects across groups rather than as a continuous correlation. Similarly, due to the high amount of participants needed to analyze the intervention-age interaction in decicion-making avoidance, we aim to examine only the main effects of age and intervention condition on decision avoidance, rather than the interaction. Our sample will be collected entirely online, rather than as a blend of in-person and online data collection. The original study found no differences between online participants and in-lab participants, so we do not expect differences for this reason. Additionally, we ask participants less questions, as the original study included a larger battery of questions used in other studies/analysis. This may result in less fatigue for the participants, which may in turn affect decision avoidance.
